title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Trauma — September 2026 (Part 2)

studies.title: Many adults who score high on autism questionnaires may be describing the effects of anxiety and a hard childhood
studies.ns_score_reason: hits a live public argument about adult autism diagnosis with real clinic data, though it is a single NHS service and correlational.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 245 consecutive first-time adult autism assessments at an NHS clinic (median age 33, 52% female), combining the Social Responsiveness Scale-2 with anxiety (GAD-7), depression (PHQ-9) and Adverse Childhood Experiences measures. Just 56.7% received a clinical autism diagnosis, and 35% of those who self-rated as strongly autistic ("experienced autism") did not meet diagnostic thresholds. High self-reported autistic traits tracked closely with anxiety and depression symptoms whether or not autism was diagnosed, and women reported more childhood adversity than men.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the questionnaires people increasingly use to understand themselves may be picking up a transdiagnostic mix of distress and adversity as well as autism — with implications for the thousands stuck on assessment waiting lists, and for what happens to those told "no".
studies.pitch_angle: Open on someone who has waited three years for an adult autism assessment, scores highly on every screening tool, and is told they are not autistic — then unpack what the questionnaire was actually measuring. Lead with the 35% figure. Call Hannah Childs and Raja Mukherjee at Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS Foundation Trust; the framing of "experienced autism" versus clinic-diagnosed autism is the intellectual hook. Avoid implying anyone's self-identification is wrong — the data cannot adjudicate individual cases.
studies.wider_angle: A longer feature for a health-policy or general-interest outlet on what adult diagnostic services are for when the queue is full of people whose difficulties are real but whose category is contested — and why so few autism clinics have any link to trauma services.
studies.caveats: Single-center NHS clinic sample; cross-sectional and observational; ACE and symptom measures self-reported; the maltreatment findings are explicitly described by the authors as hypothesis-generating; clinic attenders may not generalize to the wider population.

studies.title: A genetic hunt for resilience finds a single variant that tracks who stays well after trauma
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely novel way of defining resilience (doing better than your own predicted trajectory) in a very large cohort; the genetic signal itself is fragile.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 12,946 surgical patients in the China Surgery and Anesthesia Cohort (mean age 52, 58.5% female), measuring depressive symptoms before surgery and at 1, 6 and 12 months afterwards. Rather than defining resilience as "low symptoms", they modeled each person's expected post-surgery score and labeled the 18% who did far better than predicted as resilient. A genome-wide association study flagged one variant, rs11766511, in the neural adhesion gene *SDK1*; in a separate cohort of 2,285 severe-trauma patients, GG carriers showed lower symptom burden than AA carriers, though the additive model fell short of significance.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes resilience as a measurable deviation from your own predicted trajectory rather than a personality trait — a methodological shift that could make a slippery concept tractable. The specific gene finding needs replication before anyone reads much into it.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is the measurement trick, not the gene: you can only see resilience if you first predict how bad someone should have felt. Open on the surgical ward as an unlikely natural experiment in trauma — a scheduled, dated, universally stressful event with a before and after. Call Huan Song's group at the West China Biomedical Big Data Center, and get an independent geneticist to say plainly how much weight one 5×10⁻⁸ hit can bear.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist genomics or *Nature*-style news outlet: the replication problem in psychiatric genetics, using this as a case study in how candidate loci for behavioral traits get announced and then quietly vanish.
studies.caveats: Observational; the replication cohort result was significant only under genotype stratification, not the additive model; depressive symptoms self-reported (PHQ-9); Chinese cohorts only, so ancestry generalizability is unknown; surgery is a specific and anticipated stressor.

studies.title: People who struggle to name their feelings think their coping is working — and it isn't
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely paradoxical, highly relatable finding with dense repeated-measures data, held back by a small sample and total reliance on self-report.
studies.the_study: Forty-nine trauma-exposed adults completed baseline measures of alexithymia (difficulty identifying and describing feelings) and then three waves of ecological momentary assessment — five prompts a day for five days, repeated across three months, yielding 2,420 observations on emotional clarity, perceived coping success, body connection and strategies like rumination and emotional hiding. Among people high in alexithymia, feeling that regulation had gone well predicted *lower* emotional clarity at the next prompt, and the combination of hiding feelings and believing it worked predicted worsening post-traumatic stress symptoms over three months.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the internal signal people use to judge whether they are coping can be systematically miscalibrated — which matters for any therapy that asks patients to report on their own regulation.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the paradox: the moment you think you've handled the feeling is the moment it gets away from you. Open with a phone buzzing five times a day asking someone how they feel — the study's own design is the scene. Call Andrea Putica at the University of Melbourne, who is candid in the paper that self-report alone cannot distinguish miscalibration from reporting bias. Frame as a line of enquiry, not advice.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on alexithymia itself for a psychology or long-read outlet — an under-discussed trait affecting roughly one in ten people, sitting at the intersection of autism research, interoception and PTSD, and increasingly suspected of being a mechanism rather than a curiosity.
studies.caveats: Small N (49); entirely self-reported outcomes with no objective index of emotional change; no control group; authors explicitly call for replication in larger samples.

studies.title: Making patients relive their trauma works outside the trial setting too — and almost nobody got worse
studies.ns_score_reason: directly challenges a widespread clinical belief that exposure therapy is too destabilizing for real-world patients; naturalistic design with a waiting-list comparison phase strengthens it.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Ninety-five adults with clinician-confirmed PTSD (mean age 35.7, 76% women, 61% with sexual trauma as the index event) received Prolonged Exposure therapy in an ordinary French outpatient clinic, averaging eight sessions. Around 76% reached scores consistent with probable remission and 80% showed clinically significant improvement, with large effects sustained at three months — far exceeding the small change seen during their own waiting-list period. Just 1% deteriorated reliably, and the dropout rate was 9.5%.
studies.why_it_matters: Clinician reluctance, not lack of evidence, is the main barrier to trauma-focused therapy reaching patients; this suggests the fear of destabilizing people by asking them to revisit the worst thing that happened to them is largely unfounded in routine care.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the gap between what the evidence says and what clinicians do — and a French clinic that closed it. Open on a therapist's first session asking a patient to narrate their assault in the present tense, and the discomfort that generates in the room. Call Eric Bui at Caen University Hospital. Note the waiting-list contrast is the analytic backbone.
studies.wider_angle: For a health-services or medical-professional outlet: why evidence-based psychotherapies diffuse so slowly across Europe compared with medication, and what implementation science says actually shifts clinician behavior.
studies.caveats: Small N (95); single-center; naturalistic with no randomized control (waiting-list phase is within-subject); outcomes partly self-reported (PCL-5, QIDS-16-SR); several authors report royalties from therapy manuals and Dr. Bui reports consulting fees from Johnson & Johnson.

studies.title: In Gaza, 94% of adults screen above the normal range for psychological distress
studies.ns_score_reason: rare on-the-ground data collected during active conflict, with a clear mechanistic finding about repeated displacement; cross-sectional and sampling is inevitably constrained.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: In August 2025, researchers based at the Islamic University of Gaza surveyed 894 adults across the Gaza Strip using the WHOQOL-BREF and PHQ-4. Quality of life was extremely low, especially in the environmental (mean 25.91/100) and psychological (35.60) domains; 94.3% scored above the normal range for distress, with about two-thirds screening positive for probable anxiety and depression. Forced relocations independently predicted worse quality of life in all four domains, and psychological distress statistically mediated 26–41% of the link between cumulative resource loss and quality of life.
studies.why_it_matters: It quantifies something usually described only anecdotally — that it is the accumulation of structural losses, particularly being displaced again and again, rather than any single terrifying event, that most erodes wellbeing in war.
studies.pitch_angle: The counterintuitive edge is the mechanism: repeated relocation hurt every domain of life, while distress explained only a quarter to two-fifths of the damage — meaning most of the harm is structural, not psychological, and no amount of therapy substitutes for housing. Open on the number of times a single family has moved. Call Bashar Aldabbour at the Islamic University of Gaza, who collected data under bombardment.
studies.wider_angle: A methods-and-ethics feature for a global-health or journalism-focused outlet on how mental health research is conducted inside an active war zone, and what conservation of resources theory predicts about recovery once fighting stops.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, so causation cannot be established; self-reported measures throughout; recruitment during active conflict means the sample cannot be assumed representative; brief four-item distress screen rather than diagnostic interview.

studies.title: Recovery from disaster does not creep up on people — it arrives in sudden jumps
studies.ns_score_reason: appealing nonlinear-dynamics framing of recovery with six weeks of intensive real-world data, though the dramatic "critical transitions" appeared in only about 6% of people.
studies.the_study: Eighty-one survivors still reporting hurricane-related stress 5–8.5 months after Hurricane Florence completed six weeks of ecological momentary assessment. Using functional data analysis and generalized additive models, the researchers showed that a person's confidence in their ability to cope and their post-traumatic stress symptoms moved together — coevolving in 91–96% of participants. About 6% showed an abrupt "self-determination violation" (collapsing coping confidence with a rapid symptom spike) and another 6% an abrupt "resurgence" in the opposite direction.
studies.why_it_matters: If coping confidence and symptoms are two ends of one coupled system, interventions aimed at either one should cascade into the other — and the sudden-transition pattern suggests some recoveries are tipping points rather than gradual improvement.
studies.pitch_angle: Sell the tipping-point image: for a minority of survivors, months of stalled recovery end in a matter of days. Open on one participant's gradient plot — the moment their curve flips. Call Charles Benight at the Lyda Hill Institute for Human Resilience, who has built self-regulation shift theory over two decades and is now testing it with nonlinear tools borrowed from ecology.
studies.wider_angle: A broader piece for a data-science or complexity-focused outlet on early-warning signals and critical transitions — the same mathematics used to anticipate ecosystem collapse and market crashes, now being pointed at individual minds.
studies.caveats: Small N (81); self-reported momentary measures; no control group or intervention; single disaster in one US region; transitions were observed in a small subset, so the headline phenomenon rests on a handful of people.

studies.title: Everyday racist stereotypes track how much physical pain Black women report — independently of their mental health
studies.ns_score_reason: first quantitative test of gendered racial microaggressions against bodily pain, with a decent sample; cross-sectional design limits how far it goes.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using ordinal logistic regression on data from 415 Black women, researchers examined links between gendered racial microaggressions, bodily pain intensity and pain interference in daily life. Greater exposure to these microaggressions was associated with more intense pain and more interference, and the associations survived adjustment for depression, anxiety, stress and trauma symptoms. The strongest single dimension was exposure to the "Angry Black Woman" stereotype.
studies.why_it_matters: It puts a number on something usually discussed as a social grievance, and suggests a pathway to physical pain that is not simply "distress makes pain worse" — relevant to the well-documented undertreatment of pain in Black patients.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the counterintuitive statistical result: the pain link did not disappear when the researchers controlled for depression and anxiety, which is where most people assume the effect must live. Open on a clinical encounter in which a woman moderates how she describes her pain to avoid being read as angry. Call Tiffany R. Williams at Tennessee State University. Be careful: this is observational and cannot show that microaggressions cause pain.
studies.wider_angle: For a medical or sociology outlet: self-silencing as a physiological variable — a feature on the emerging evidence that how freely people are able to report symptoms shapes both their treatment and, potentially, their physiology.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational; all measures self-reported; US sample of Black women recruited for this purpose, so generalizability unclear; mediation and directionality cannot be resolved with these data.

studies.title: Virtual reality role-play helps adults with difficult childhoods read faces again
studies.ns_score_reason: first intervention to directly target social cognition in adults with childhood trauma, with a large effect size, but it is an uncontrolled pilot.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Thirty-two adults with histories of early-life adversity and ongoing social difficulties were offered SOCIAbLE, an eight-session program combining psychoeducation, cognitive-behavioral strategies and immersive VR social role-play; 25 completed it and 24 returned at 18 weeks. Emotion recognition on the BLERT improved substantially by 12 weeks (g = 1.04) and gains held at 18 weeks, alongside improvements in symptoms and social function. Interviews indicated high acceptability, with participants reporting gains in confidence and real-world socializing.
studies.why_it_matters: Difficulty reading other people is one of the most persistent and least treated legacies of childhood adversity; this is the first attempt to train it directly, and the effect is large enough to justify a proper randomized trial.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is that a deficit usually treated as a fixed scar of childhood shifted in eight hours of practice — in a headset. Open on a participant rehearsing a job interview with an avatar who keeps giving them ambiguous looks. Call Gary Donohoe at the University of Galway; Daniel Freeman at Oxford, a co-author and the leading figure in VR therapy, is the natural second call. Do not imply this is available treatment — it is a proof of concept.
studies.wider_angle: A trend piece for a technology or health-business outlet on VR therapy's second act: after a wave of hype for phobias and psychosis, what has actually survived to randomized trials, and what the headset-based therapy market looks like now.
studies.caveats: Small N (32 baseline, 23–25 completers); single-arm with no control group, so expectancy and repeated testing cannot be ruled out; single site; short follow-up (18 weeks); outcomes partly self-reported.

studies.title: Shame, not guilt, is what cuts trauma survivors off from the people around them
studies.ns_score_reason: a very large sample from an under-studied population and a clean shame/guilt dissociation, but cross-sectional self-report mediation.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed questionnaire data from 3,419 Arabic-speaking, treatment-seeking women with histories of sexual violence who registered for an online intervention. Higher PTSD symptoms went with lower perceived social support, and in a parallel mediation model trauma-related shame was the dominant explanatory route. Guilt cognitions showed a small indirect effect in the *opposite* direction, and self-blame showed none at all.
studies.why_it_matters: Shame and guilt are routinely lumped together in trauma care, yet here they pull in opposite directions — suggesting the two emotions do different things to a survivor's connection with other people.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the dissociation: shame isolates, guilt very slightly does the reverse. The distinction — "I did a bad thing" versus "I am a bad thing" — is the piece's spine, and it is the kind of idea readers can immediately apply to themselves. Call Maria Böttche or Christine Knaevelsrud at Freie Universität Berlin, who run the online intervention that generated this dataset. Keep it descriptive; the design cannot show shame causes withdrawal.
studies.wider_angle: For a global-health or Middle East-focused outlet: what it takes to deliver trauma treatment in Arabic at scale online, and what a 3,400-strong self-referral queue says about unmet need among displaced and refugee women.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, so the mediation is statistical rather than causal; all self-report; treatment-seeking online sample will not represent survivors generally; effect sizes modest (β = −0.21 for the main association).

studies.title: When a mother's trauma reaches her child, it travels through the stress of parenting
studies.ns_score_reason: a specific, testable pathway with an objective child cognitive measure, but cross-sectional and single-author.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Two hundred Syrian refugee mother–child dyads in Mardin, Türkiye (children aged 6–11) completed measures of maternal PTSD, parenting stress, depression and anxiety, child emotional and behavioral problems, and — for children — the Stroop test of inhibitory control. Parenting stress statistically mediated the link between maternal PTSD symptoms and both child behavioral problems and Stroop interference, holding after adjustment for maternal depression and anxiety. Interviews with 30 dyads described the same pattern: exhaustion, irritability and inconsistent responsiveness, with warmth, school support and religious coping acting as buffers.
studies.why_it_matters: "Intergenerational trauma" is usually invoked vaguely; this points at a concrete, potentially modifiable relay — day-to-day parenting strain — and links it to a measurable cognitive outcome in the child rather than just behavior ratings.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is the Stroop result: a mother's post-traumatic stress showed up in her child's measured attention control, not just in how she rated the child's behavior. Open on a mother in Mardin describing how she knows her temper has changed. Call Metin Çınaroğlu at İstanbul Nişantaşı University. Frame the mediation carefully — this is one cross-sectional snapshot.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a development or humanitarian outlet arguing that child mental health programs in refugee settings are aimed at the wrong person, and reviewing the small number of caregiver-first trials that have tested this.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, so mediation cannot establish causal sequence; maternal reports supply both the predictor and most outcomes (shared-method variance); single site and single author; no control group of non-displaced dyads.

studies.title: The trauma-exposed brain's sensory-to-thinking hierarchy is reorganized — and differently in teenagers
studies.ns_score_reason: strong design with trauma-exposed controls who survived the same disaster, but the gene-expression and neurotransmitter overlays are correlational map-matching.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using resting-state fMRI, researchers compared 86 adults with non-comorbid PTSD following an earthquake against 86 people who lived through the same earthquake without developing PTSD. The PTSD group showed altered organization of the brain's principal gradient running from sensory to abstract-thinking regions, with focal changes in visual, limbic, ventral attention and frontoparietal networks. Sex made no difference, but subcortical gradient reductions were more pronounced in adolescents than adults, and the affected regions overlapped with gene expression related to mitochondrial and nucleic-acid metabolism and with dopamine, opioid, noradrenaline and cholinergic receptor maps.
studies.why_it_matters: The matched trauma-exposed control group means these differences are about developing PTSD rather than about surviving a disaster — a distinction most imaging studies cannot make.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the control group: everyone in this study lived through the same earthquake, so the brain differences separate those who developed PTSD from those who did not. Add the age twist — the subcortical effect was bigger in adolescents, hinting that when trauma arrives matters as much as what it is. Call Xueling Suo or Qiyong Gong at West China Hospital. Resist any biomarker claims; group-level differences do not diagnose individuals.
studies.wider_angle: For a neuroscience-specialist outlet: the rise of "gradient" approaches to the connectome, and the methodological debate over whether overlaying group brain maps onto post-mortem gene-expression atlases can really tell us anything mechanistic.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional; moderate sample by imaging standards; transcriptomic and neurotransmitter associations rest on spatial correlation with external reference atlases, not measurements in these participants; single disaster and single population.

studies.title: What actually protects child protection workers from secondary trauma is not what protects them from burnout
studies.ns_score_reason: large, careful meta-analysis that pulls apart two conditions usually treated as one, though built almost entirely on cross-sectional studies.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A systematic search to May 2026 yielded 84 studies (72 independent samples, 592 effect sizes) on burnout and secondary traumatic stress among child protection workers. Some factors mattered for both — age, resilience, self-care, network support, supervisor and organizational support all protective; workload, role stress and work-family conflict all harmful. But several diverged sharply: workload, autonomy, financial reward and problem-focused coping were more strongly tied to burnout, while the worker's own trauma history, avoidance coping, on-the-job trauma exposure and coworker support were more strongly tied to secondary traumatic stress.
studies.why_it_matters: Organizations tend to treat staff distress as one problem with one solution; this indicates that fixing caseloads addresses burnout while doing little for the distinct, trauma-driven condition that pushes people out of the profession.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the split: giving an overwhelmed social worker a lighter caseload may be the wrong lever entirely if the problem is secondary traumatic stress. Open on a worker who carries other people's worst days home. Call Jorien Roest at the University of Applied Sciences Leiden. The finding that workers' own trauma histories predicted secondary stress specifically is the most sensitive — and most quotable — result.
studies.wider_angle: For a workplace or public-services outlet: a piece on trauma-exposed professions generally — 999 call handlers, content moderators, asylum caseworkers, court transcribers — and whether any employer has built a policy that distinguishes overwork from vicarious trauma.
studies.caveats: Most included studies were cross-sectional, so "risk" and "protective" factors are correlates, not established causes; self-reported measures throughout; heterogeneity across 72 samples and national contexts; publication bias possible.

studies.title: Teenagers who try suicide again are not flagged by the obvious warning signs
studies.ns_score_reason: a prospective clinical cohort with a year of follow-up and a genuinely awkward negative result, though network analysis is hard to translate for general readers.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: As part of Spain's SURVIVE consortium, researchers recruited 287 adolescents aged 12–17 treated in emergency departments after a suicide attempt and followed them for a year, mapping clinical interview and questionnaire data as a network. Emotional and behavioral difficulties, childhood trauma and depressive symptoms were the most central nodes — but reattempts and their frequency sat at the network's periphery with no significant direct connections. Emotional abuse was associated with a higher lifetime number of attempts, and a Self-Awareness of Mental Health intervention was linked to a longer interval before reattempt.
studies.why_it_matters: It undercuts the assumption that reattempt risk can be read off a checklist of the usual risk factors, supporting a shift toward modeling how factors interact rather than which single one predicts.
studies.pitch_angle: The story is the null: in a network of everything clinicians measure in teenagers after an attempt, "will they do it again" floated free of all of it. Open in a hospital emergency department with a clinician filling out a risk form they know does not work. Call Pilar A. Saiz at the University of Oviedo. Handle with standard suicide-reporting care and no suggestion that risk assessment should be abandoned.
studies.wider_angle: For a health-policy or investigative outlet: the accumulating evidence that structured suicide risk-stratification tools perform poorly, and why health systems keep mandating them anyway.
studies.caveats: Observational; N = 287 with one year of follow-up limits statistical power for a relatively rare outcome; Spanish clinical sample only; self-report instruments used for most variables; network analysis findings are exploratory and require replication.

studies.title: Mothers who were maltreated as children feel like objects while breastfeeding — and it shows in the room
studies.journal: Journal of Reproductive and Infant Psychology
studies.ns_score_reason: striking, intimate idea backed by blind-coded video observation rather than questionnaires alone, but this is an underpowered pilot with unstable findings.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Fifty women up to six months postpartum (35 reporting childhood maltreatment, 15 not) completed self-report questionnaires and were video-recorded breastfeeding, with the footage coded for Emotional Availability by trained certified raters. Self-objectification — viewing one's own body as an object — was associated with lower observed emotional availability and more negative feelings about breastfeeding, and statistically linked childhood maltreatment to negative breastfeeding feelings. The equivalent indirect path to observed emotional availability held under some analytic methods but not others, and group differences in emotional availability categories were not significant, though maternal detachment was more common in the maltreatment group (31.4% vs 6.7%).
studies.why_it_matters: It proposes a specific psychological route — feeling like a body being used rather than a person feeding a baby — from childhood maltreatment to the quality of early mother-infant interaction, in a domain dominated by research on duration and nutrition.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a mother who wanted to breastfeed, is breastfeeding, and feels absent while doing it — then explain why self-objectification might be the missing variable in breastfeeding research obsessed with how long and how much. Call Anat Talmon at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Be explicit that this is a pilot whose central mediation was not robust across methods.
studies.wider_angle: For a parenting or women's health outlet: the pressure to breastfeed meets trauma history — a feature on why "breast is best" messaging lands very differently on women with histories of abuse, and what trauma-informed postnatal support would actually look like.
studies.caveats: Small N (50, with only 15 in the comparison group); pilot study; key indirect effect unstable across inferential methods; group comparison non-significant; self-reported maltreatment and self-objectification; single site.

studies.title: Self-harm in psychosis has different roots depending on whether the patient is in a forensic unit
studies.ns_score_reason: multinational sample and a clean divergence in risk profiles, but a specialist clinical topic that is a hard sell for general readers.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Drawing on the EU-VIORMED study across five European countries, researchers compared 392 patients aged 18–65 with schizophrenia spectrum disorders, split into forensic and non-forensic groups, and used LASSO logistic regression to identify correlates of lifetime deliberate self-harm. Prevalence was similarly high in both (45.9% forensic, 39.5% non-forensic), but the drivers diverged: comorbid personality disorder and functional impairment dominated in forensic patients, whereas interpersonal victimization was the single strongest correlate in non-forensic patients, followed by personality disorder, male gender and substance use.
studies.why_it_matters: Same diagnosis, same rate of self-harm, different underlying pattern — an argument against one-size-fits-all risk formulation in psychosis services, and a reminder that being a victim of violence is a strong signal in a group usually discussed as perpetrators.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the inversion: in the non-forensic group, having been victimized by others predicted self-harm more strongly than any symptom of psychosis did. Open on the statistic that nearly half of forensic patients with schizophrenia have harmed themselves. Call Giovanni de Girolamo at IRCCS Fatebenefratelli in Brescia, who leads EU-VIORMED.
studies.wider_angle: For a criminal-justice or public-health outlet: victimization rates among people with severe mental illness, and why secure services are set up to assess the risk patients pose to others but not the risk others have posed to them.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional with lifetime self-harm measured dichotomously; observational, so correlates are not causes; LASSO coefficients are selection-dependent and not directly interpretable as effect sizes; European secure and community services may not generalize.

studies.title: Racism and sexism push men and women toward addiction after trauma by opposite routes
studies.ns_score_reason: a sharp gendered contrast in an under-researched comorbidity, but a small qualitative study that cannot quantify anything.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers conducted in-depth qualitative interviews with 23 people of color living with co-occurring PTSD and substance use disorder. Women described sexism shaping their exposure to sexual violence and expectations of being disbelieved or blamed — because of both gender and race — driving substance use as a way to cope. Men described racism increasing their exposure to gang, gun and interpersonal violence, gender stereotypes requiring them to "tough it out", and criminalization making it unsafe to ask for help with either trauma or substance use.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers a concrete account of *how* interlocking disadvantages translate into one of the most treatment-resistant comorbidities in psychiatry, which quantitative studies of the same association rarely supply.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is that the same two forces produced two mirror-image pathways to the same diagnosis pair. Open on a man who could not report being shot at without risking arrest himself. Call Nicole Buchanan at Michigan State University. Present as hypothesis-generating testimony, not epidemiology.
studies.wider_angle: For a US public-health or social-policy outlet: why PTSD and addiction are so often treated in separate, sequential services that require patients to be sober before trauma therapy, and what integrated-treatment trials have shown.
studies.caveats: Small N (23); qualitative, so no prevalence or effect estimates; US-specific racial and legal context; retrospective accounts of causation from participants themselves; single research team conducting analysis.

citation_table.journal: Journal of Reproductive and Infant Psychology

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- **Alexithymia is consolidating as a mechanism rather than a curiosity.** "People who struggle to name their feelings think their coping is working — and it isn't" (PMID 42721324) sits directly alongside last run's "Trouble naming your feelings may link childhood trauma to a stiffer heartbeat" (PMID 42579979). One links poor emotional clarity to autonomic rigidity, the other to systematically miscalibrated self-monitoring; together they make a stronger case than either alone that difficulty labeling emotion is doing causal work in post-traumatic outcomes.
- **Self-conscious emotions and self-concept keep separating out into distinct routes.** "Shame, not guilt, is what cuts trauma survivors off from the people around them" (PMID 42766479) extends the previous digest's two dissociation papers — "trauma identity" versus safety-seeking after the Kahramanmaraş earthquakes (PMID 42036873) and perpetration-based moral injury tracking depersonalization in Israeli veterans (PMID 41347711). Three consecutive months of evidence that emotions routinely bundled together in trauma care behave differently.
- **The standard clinical variables keep failing to predict the outcomes clinicians care about.** "Teenagers who try suicide again are not flagged by the obvious warning signs" (PMID 42734150) echoes both "Psychiatric diagnoses barely predict how patients actually fare" (PMID 42644771) and "Who drops out of trauma treatment isn't predicted by how ill they are" (PMID 42222912).
- **Minority stress and victimization as trauma exposures.** "Everyday racist stereotypes track how much physical pain Black women report" (PMID 42721338), "Racism and sexism push men and women toward addiction after trauma by opposite routes" (PMID 42708575) and "Self-harm in psychosis has different roots depending on whether the patient is in a forensic unit" (PMID 42711065) all build on last run's meta-analysis of rejection and violence in trans people (PMID 42658623).

**Advances**
- **Where the diagnostic line sits, now applied to autism.** "Many adults who score high on autism questionnaires may be describing the effects of anxiety and a hard childhood" (PMID 42772961) takes last run's PTSD-boundary thread (PMID 42635035, 42635367) into a neighboring, noisier public argument — the same problem of self-report instruments capturing transdiagnostic distress, in a diagnosis with far larger waiting lists.
- **Understudied trauma-exposed populations.** Last run brought in unattended children in China (PMID 42594693), Lahore slum children (PMID 41974448) and refugee young adults in Sweden (PMID 42635367). This run adds adults surveyed inside Gaza during active conflict (PMID 42728821), Syrian refugee mother–child dyads in Türkiye (PMID 42760574) and 3,419 Arabic-speaking survivors of sexual violence (PMID 42766479) — with a marked shift toward structural exposures rather than index events.
- **Early adversity as modifiable, not fixed.** Last run's chronic pain cohort showed high-ACE patients improved as much as everyone else (PMID 42166956); "Virtual reality role-play helps adults with difficult childhoods read faces again" (PMID 42765386) goes further, moving a social-cognitive deficit usually treated as a permanent scar.

**Counterpoints**
- **Dropout and deterioration numbers pull in opposite directions.** "Making patients relive their trauma works outside the trial setting too" (PMID 42766476) reports 9.5% dropout and 1% reliable deterioration in routine French outpatient care, against 43.4% premature departure in last run's Israeli inpatient PTSD/eating disorder sample (PMID 42222912). Read together, they suggest disengagement is a function of setting and comorbidity rather than of exposure therapy itself — a usable tension for a reporter.

**New themes**
- **Intensive within-person time series and nonlinear modeling.** "Recovery from disaster does not creep up on people — it arrives in sudden jumps" (PMID 42715666), the alexithymia EMA study (PMID 42721324) and the redefinition of resilience as deviation from one's own predicted trajectory (PMID 42765393) all abandon group averages. Nothing comparable appeared last run.
- **Biology returns in two forms absent from the previous digest:** a genome-wide hit for resilience (PMID 42765393) and cortical gradient reorganization in PTSD against trauma-exposed controls (PMID 42740407).
- **Occupational and vicarious trauma:** "What actually protects child protection workers from secondary trauma is not what protects them from burnout" (PMID 42732758) opens a workforce strand with no precedent in the last run.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Several studies this month locate post-traumatic harm in conditions that are still happening rather than in an event that has finished — and, strikingly, find that psychological distress accounts for only part of the damage. In Gaza, repeated forced relocation independently predicted worse quality of life in all four domains, with distress mediating just 26–41% of the effect of cumulative resource loss (PMID 42728821); Black women's bodily pain tracked exposure to gendered racial microaggressions even after adjustment for depression, anxiety, stress and trauma symptoms (PMID 42721338); interpersonal victimization was the single strongest correlate of self-harm in non-forensic psychosis patients (PMID 42711065); qualitative interviews traced racism and sexism into two mirror-image routes to co-occurring PTSD and addiction (PMID 42708575); and maternal post-traumatic stress reached Syrian refugee children through the daily grind of parenting stress, showing up in their measured attention control (PMID 42760574). Even the workforce paper fits: what drove secondary traumatic stress in child protection workers was on-the-job trauma exposure and their own histories, not the caseload that drives burnout (PMID 42732758).

**Why pitch this now:** Trauma-informed care is being adopted across health systems, schools and aid agencies at the same moment as this evidence suggests the psychological pathway is the minority share of the harm — which makes it a question about where money and political attention should go, not just a clinical one.

**Angle:** A reported feature that takes the mediation arithmetic seriously — follow the numbers from a Gaza survey conducted under bombardment through a US pain clinic and a European secure unit, asking what proportion of measured harm therapy can plausibly reach and what the rest would require. For general science readers who have absorbed the language of trauma but not the finding that most of the damage may sit outside the mind.

**Potential headlines:**
- Ongoing conditions, not past events, are what trauma clinics keep measuring
- Most of what war does to wellbeing never passes through the mind
- The trauma treatments that cannot reach the cause

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the mediation percentages and the Gaza and microaggression data give it a quantitative spine that suits a long Mind-adjacent feature rather than a news item.
- **The Guardian science desk** — would run the conflict and racial-health strands together, with the Gaza fieldwork as the news peg.
- **Undark** — natural home for a piece on how research conducted inside a war zone reframes what mental health aid is supposed to deliver.
- **Nature** news features — the methodological question of what mediation analysis can and cannot establish about structural versus psychological harm has an audience among global mental health researchers.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Trauma — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-24 | **Studies reviewed:** 16
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run 2026-09-24

---

### Study 1: Many adults who score high on autism questionnaires may be describing the effects of anxiety and a hard childhood
**PMID:** 42772961 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Sample (245 consecutive NHS first adult assessments), median age 33, 52% female, 56.7% diagnosed, 35% of "experienced autism" adults below threshold (64/181), internalising link "regardless of CA", ACE–female sex association — all match the abstract. Caveats correctly reproduce the authors' "hypothesis-generating" language on maltreatment.

**Issue A. Headline gives childhood adversity equal billing with anxiety** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Many adults who score high on autism questionnaires may be describing the effects of anxiety and a hard childhood"
- **Abstract says:** "Cumulative ACE scores did not distinguish EA/CA groups but were independently associated with female sex (p = .012)."
- **Problem:** The internalising (GAD-7/PHQ-9) association with high self-reported traits is strong and explicit (all p ⩽ .002); the adversity component is not — cumulative ACE scores did *not* separate the groups. The authors' lay abstract does use similar phrasing, so this is an echo of the paper rather than an invention, but a headline that pairs anxiety and "a hard childhood" as co-equal explanations runs ahead of the statistics.
- **Suggested fix:** "Many adults who score high on autism questionnaires may be describing the effects of anxiety and low mood"

**Note on NS fit (7/10):** Defensible. The outcome (autism diagnosis) is clinician-determined rather than self-reported, N is respectable and the topic is live. No change recommended.

---

### Study 2: A genetic hunt for resilience finds a single variant that tracks who stays well after trauma
**PMID:** 42765393 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Cohort size (12,946), mean age 52.2, 58.5% female, PHQ-9 at pre-surgery and 1/6/12 months, 18.0% resilient, rs11766511 mapped to *SDK1*, replication in 2,285 CSTC patients, GG vs AA genotype-stratified result, non-significant additive model — all accurate, and the caveats correctly flag the additive-model failure.

**Issue A. P-value shorthand misstates the reported statistic** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "get an independent geneticist to say plainly how much weight one 5×10⁻⁸ hit can bear"
- **Abstract says:** "GWAS identified a lead single-nucleotide polymorphism (rs11766511, P = 3.082 × 10-8)"
- **Problem:** 5×10⁻⁸ is the conventional genome-wide significance *threshold*, not this study's P value. Written as "one 5×10⁻⁸ hit" a writer could reproduce it as the result.
- **Suggested fix:** "…how much weight one hit at P = 3.1×10⁻⁸ — barely past the genome-wide threshold — can bear"

**Issue B. NS fit score sits on the weakest part of the paper** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — a genuinely novel way of defining resilience… the genetic signal itself is fragile."
- **Problem:** The score note justifies 7 on the methodology, but the headline sells the variant. The variant survives replication only under genotype stratification, the additive model is null, and the authors themselves say the locus "warrants confirmation." A 7 attached to a headline about a single unconfirmed candidate locus is optimistic.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 6/10, or keep 7/10 only if the headline is rewritten around the measurement method ("A new way of measuring resilience: doing better than your own predicted trajectory").

---

### Study 3: People who struggle to name their feelings think their coping is working — and it isn't
**PMID:** 42721324 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 49, three EMA waves, five prompts/day for five days across three months, 2,420 observations, lagged finding that perceived regulation success predicted lower next-assessment emotional clarity among high-alexithymia participants, and hiding + perceived success predicting worsening PTSS — all match.

**Issue A. Headline asserts what the authors say they cannot determine** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "People who struggle to name their feelings think their coping is working — and it isn't"
- **Abstract says:** "whether it reflects miscalibrated evaluation, divergent regulatory goals, or systematic reporting biases cannot be determined from self-report alone"
- **Problem:** "And it isn't" states that the regulation genuinely failed. The data show a self-reported paradox; the authors explicitly decline to say which of three explanations it is. The pitch text handles this well, but the headline does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "People who struggle to name their feelings say their coping is working — just before things get worse"

**Issue B. Prevalence figure not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "an under-discussed trait affecting roughly one in ten people"
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. Commonly cited, but it needs sourcing before it reaches a pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** Attribute to a named prevalence source or drop the figure.

---

### Study 4: Making patients relive their trauma works outside the trial setting too — and almost nobody got worse
**PMID:** 42766476 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

N = 95, CAPS-5-confirmed PTSD, mean age 35.65, 76% women, 61% sexual trauma index event, mean 8 sessions, 75.53% probable remission, 79.78% clinically significant improvement, 1% reliable worsening, 9.47% dropout, waiting-list d = 0.33 — all accurately rendered. Industry/royalty disclosures are correctly carried into Caveats.

**Issue A. Headline claims efficacy from an uncontrolled naturalistic study** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Making patients relive their trauma works outside the trial setting too"
- **Abstract says:** "These findings suggest that PE may be feasibly and safely delivered in routine outpatient care and may be associated with substantial reductions in PTSD symptoms."
- **Problem:** "Works" is an efficacy claim. The design is single-arm and naturalistic; the waiting-list contrast is within-subject, not randomized, so it cannot exclude regression to the mean, natural recovery or expectancy. The authors twice hedge with "may."
- **Suggested fix:** "Exposure therapy delivered safely in an ordinary French clinic — and almost nobody got worse"

**Issue B. Novelty label does not match what the study did** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research"
- **Abstract says:** PE has "well-established efficacy in randomised controlled trials. However, its implementation in routine care remains limited."
- **Problem:** The study is consistent with, not contrary to, prior research; what it challenges is clinician practice and belief. "Overturns prior research" would mislead an editor about the paper's standing.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** Confirms in the real world / challenges clinical practice"

**Issue C. Cause of the implementation gap asserted, not measured** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Clinician reluctance, not lack of evidence, is the main barrier to trauma-focused therapy reaching patients"
- **Abstract says:** Implementation "remains limited, particularly in outpatient clinics where evidence-based psychotherapies are not widely adopted."
- **Problem:** The study did not measure why clinicians do or don't deliver PE. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Trauma-focused therapy remains under-delivered in routine outpatient care; this study suggests safety concerns are not a good reason for that."

---

### Study 5: In Gaza, 94% of adults screen above the normal range for psychological distress
**PMID:** 42728821 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

August 2025 survey, 894 adults, WHOQOL-BREF and PHQ-4, environmental 25.91 and psychological 35.60, 94.3% above normal range, 64.9%/65.5% probable anxiety/depression, forced relocations associated with lower QoL across all four domains — all accurate.

**Issue A. Pitch inverts the abstract's emphasis on distress** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "distress explained only a quarter to two-fifths of the damage — meaning most of the harm is structural, not psychological, and no amount of therapy substitutes for housing"
- **Abstract says:** "psychological distress was the strongest and most consistent predictor of reduced QoL across all domains (β range: -1.67 to -2.28…)" and "Integrated humanitarian responses that address both structural restoration and scalable mental health interventions are urgently needed."
- **Problem:** The 26–41% figures describe only the mediated portion of the *resource-loss* pathway; they are not a share of total harm. The authors name distress as the strongest single predictor of QoL and call for both structural and mental health responses. The pitch converts a partial-mediation statistic into a policy conclusion the paper argues against.
- **Suggested fix:** "Distress accounted for roughly a quarter to two-fifths of the link between cumulative loss and quality of life — so resource loss also damaged wellbeing directly, and the authors argue structural restoration and mental health support are both needed."

**Issue B. Headline generalizes a convenience sample to a population** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "In Gaza, 94% of adults screen above the normal range for psychological distress"
- **Abstract says:** "cross-sectional survey in August 2025 among 894 adults across the Gaza Strip… 94.3% scoring above the normal range"
- **Problem:** The headline reads as a population estimate; the digest's own Caveats state the sample "cannot be assumed representative." Headline and caveat contradict each other.
- **Suggested fix:** "In a survey of nearly 900 adults in Gaza, 94% screened above the normal range for psychological distress"

**Issue C. Mediation percentages conflated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "psychological distress statistically mediated 26–41% of the link between cumulative resource loss and quality of life"
- **Abstract says:** "accounting for 26% of the association with overall QoL and 29%-41% of the association with domain-specific outcomes"
- **Problem:** 26% is the overall-QoL figure; the domain-specific range starts at 29%. Presented as a single 26–41% band it slightly misdescribes the analysis.
- **Suggested fix:** "mediated 26% of the link with overall quality of life and 29–41% of the domain-specific links"

---

### Study 6: Recovery from disaster does not creep up on people — it arrives in sudden jumps
**PMID:** 42715666 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

N = 81, 5–8.5 months after Hurricane Florence, six weeks of EMA, functional data analysis plus generalized additive modelling, coevolution in 91–96%, ~6% self-determination violation and ~6% resurgence — all accurate, and the NS fit note and Caveats both flag the 6%.

**Issue A. Headline states as general what the study found in a small minority** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Recovery from disaster does not creep up on people — it arrives in sudden jumps"
- **Abstract says:** "approximately 6% of survivors exhibited nonlinear transitions consistent with SRST's self-determination violation and an additional 6% exhibited nonlinear transitions consistent with SRST's self-determination resurgence."
- **Problem:** Roughly 88% of participants showed neither abrupt transition. The headline asserts the opposite of what the data show for most survivors, and the abstract itself calls the support "preliminary." The pitch text correctly says "for a minority of survivors," so headline and body are inconsistent.
- **Suggested fix:** "For some disaster survivors, recovery doesn't creep up — it arrives in a sudden jump"

---

### Study 7: Everyday racist stereotypes track how much physical pain Black women report — independently of their mental health
**PMID:** 42721338 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N = 415, ordinal logistic regression, association of gendered racial microaggressions with both pain intensity and pain interference, persistence after controlling for depression, anxiety, stress and trauma symptoms, and the Angry Black Woman Stereotype as the strongest dimension all match the abstract. "Track" and "associated with" keep the framing correlational, the pitch explicitly warns against causal reading, and the Caveats cover cross-sectional design and self-report.

---

### Study 8: Virtual reality role-play helps adults with difficult childhoods read faces again
**PMID:** 42765386 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

Attrition figures (32 baseline, 25 completing the 8-week intervention, 24 at 18 weeks), eight weekly one-hour sessions, BLERT g = 1.04 at 12 weeks, persistence at 18 weeks, qualitative acceptability — all accurate. Freeman's co-authorship is correct.

**Issue A. Headline makes a causal efficacy claim from a single-arm pilot** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Virtual reality role-play helps adults with difficult childhoods read faces again"
- **Abstract says:** "This single-arm proof-of-concept study… SOCIAbLE was observed to be feasible and acceptable and showed preliminary evidence of benefits… warrant further investigation in a full randomized controlled trial."
- **Problem:** "Helps" attributes the improvement to the intervention. With no control arm, practice effects on the BLERT, expectancy and regression to the mean are all live alternatives — which is precisely why the authors call for an RCT. The pitch correctly says "proof of concept," so the headline undercuts the body.
- **Suggested fix:** "A VR role-play pilot improved emotion recognition in adults with childhood trauma — enough to justify a proper trial"

**Issue B. "First attempt" and "read faces" both slightly overstate** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this is the first attempt to train it directly" / "read faces again"
- **Abstract says:** "these difficulties are rarely therapeutically targeted"; the primary outcome is "BLERT emotional recognition"
- **Problem:** "Rarely targeted" is not "never attempted." The BLERT presents emotion across face, voice and gesture, so "read faces" narrows the outcome measure.
- **Suggested fix:** "difficulties that are rarely targeted therapeutically… improved emotion recognition"

---

### Study 9: Shame, not guilt, is what cuts trauma survivors off from the people around them
**PMID:** 42766479 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

N = 3,419, Arabic-speaking treatment-seeking women with sexual violence histories registering for an online intervention, β = −0.21 for PTSD–social support, shame as dominant mediator, guilt's small opposite-direction indirect effect, no significant self-blame effect — all accurate.

**Issue A. Headline is causal and generalized beyond the study population** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Shame, not guilt, is what cuts trauma survivors off from the people around them"
- **Abstract says:** "These findings suggest that trauma-related shame may play a role in the relationship between PTSD symptoms and perceived social support among women with a history of sexual violence exposure"
- **Problem:** Two problems in one line: "cuts… off" is causal language for a cross-sectional mediation, and "trauma survivors" extends a finding from Arabic-speaking female sexual-violence survivors seeking online treatment to survivors in general. The pitch text says "the design cannot show shame causes withdrawal," so the headline contradicts the digest's own guidance. Note also the outcome is *perceived* social support, not actual isolation.
- **Suggested fix:** "Shame, not guilt, tracks with feeling unsupported in women who have survived sexual violence"

**Issue B. Sample described as displaced and refugee women** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "what a 3,400-strong self-referral queue says about unmet need among displaced and refugee women"
- **Abstract says:** "Arabic-speaking, treatment-seeking women with a history of sexual violence exposure who registered for an online intervention"
- **Problem:** Displacement/refugee status is not reported in the abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "unmet need among Arabic-speaking women survivors"

---

### Study 10: When a mother's trauma reaches her child, it travels through the stress of parenting
**PMID:** 42760574 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 200 Syrian refugee dyads in Mardin, children 6–11, PCL-5/PSI-SF/BDI-II/GAD-7/CBCL plus child Stroop, significant mediated effects on CBCL Total Problems and Stroop interference with covariates, 30-dyad qualitative subsample, buffers including warmth, school support and religious coping, single author — all accurate.

**Issue A. Headline asserts a causal relay** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "When a mother's trauma reaches her child, it travels through the stress of parenting"
- **Abstract says:** "parenting stress may represent an important relational pathway linking maternal trauma-related distress with children's… functioning"
- **Problem:** "Travels through" presents a cross-sectional statistical mediation as an established mechanism with a direction of flow. The body text and Caveats are careful; the headline is not.
- **Suggested fix:** "A mother's trauma and her child's attention: parenting stress may be the link"

---

### Study 11: The trauma-exposed brain's sensory-to-thinking hierarchy is reorganized — and differently in teenagers
**PMID:** 42740407 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

86 non-comorbid PTSD vs 86 trauma-exposed non-PTSD controls from the same earthquake, principal unimodal-to-transmodal gradient abnormalities, focal changes in visual, limbic, ventral attention and frontoparietal networks, no sex effect, subcortical decrease more prominent in adolescents, transcriptomic enrichment and neurotransmitter colocalization — all accurate. The Caveats correctly note that the gene-expression and receptor maps are spatial correlations with external atlases.

**Issue A. "Adults" and "adolescents" cannot both be right** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "researchers compared 86 adults with non-comorbid PTSD following an earthquake" … "subcortical gradient reductions were more pronounced in adolescents than adults"
- **Abstract says:** "86 non-comorbid adult patients with PTSD caused by an earthquake" … "gradient decrease in the subcortical network is more prominent in adolescents with PTSD than adults"
- **Problem:** The abstract itself is internally inconsistent — it describes an all-adult patient sample and then reports an adolescent subgroup. The digest faithfully reproduces both, but a pitch built on "the age twist" needs the actual age range and subgroup sizes, which are unverifiable from the abstract alone.
- **Suggested fix:** Check the full text for the sample age range and adolescent subgroup n before pitching; if unresolved, drop the adolescent angle to a secondary mention.

---

### Study 12: What actually protects child protection workers from secondary trauma is not what protects them from burnout
**PMID:** 42732758 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

84 studies, 72 independent samples, 592 effect sizes, search to May 2026, shared and divergent correlates all correctly assigned to burnout vs STS. Caveats correctly state that cross-sectional design means these are correlates, matching the abstract's own closing sentence. (The digest omits compassion satisfaction and emotion-focused coping from the divergent list — an omission, not an error.)

**Issue A. Turnover attributed specifically to secondary traumatic stress** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "fixing caseloads addresses burnout while doing little for the distinct, trauma-driven condition that pushes people out of the profession"
- **Abstract says:** "These conditions threaten their well-being and service provision, and may lead to increased turnover rates"
- **Problem:** The abstract attributes possible turnover to both burnout and STS; the digest assigns it to STS alone, which sharpens the story beyond the evidence.
- **Suggested fix:** "…does little for the distinct, trauma-driven condition sitting alongside it"

---

### Study 13: Teenagers who try suicide again are not flagged by the obvious warning signs
**PMID:** 42734150 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

287 adolescents aged 12–17 recruited after an emergency-department-treated attempt, one-year follow-up, SURVIVE consortium, central nodes (emotional/behavioural difficulties, childhood trauma, depressive symptoms), reattempts peripheral with no significant direct associations, emotional abuse linked to higher lifetime attempt count, Self-Awareness of Mental Health intervention linked to longer time to reattempt — all accurate. Suicide-reporting care is appropriately flagged.

**Issue A. Scene-setting asserts that risk tools don't work** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Open in a hospital emergency department with a clinician filling out a risk form they know does not work."
- **Abstract says:** "Incorporating standardized self-report tools may enhance clinical assessment and prevention strategies."
- **Problem:** The authors' own conclusion is pro-instrument; the study found that reattempt nodes were peripheral in an exploratory network, which is not a test of any risk-assessment tool's performance. The suggested scene puts a claim in a clinician's head that this paper does not support — and it sits oddly next to the digest's own instruction not to suggest abandoning risk assessment.
- **Suggested fix:** "Open in a hospital emergency department with a clinician completing a post-attempt risk assessment — then ask what the network analysis says about which of those items connect to what happens next."

---

### Study 14: Mothers who were maltreated as children feel like objects while breastfeeding — and it shows in the room
**PMID:** 42711662 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

N = 50 (35 CM, 15 non-CM), up to six months postpartum, video-coded Emotional Availability by certified raters, self-objectification associated with lower observed EA and more negative breastfeeding feelings, indirect path to negative feelings supported, indirect path to observed EA differing across inferential methods, omnibus p = .244 with Cramér's V = .29, detachment 31.4% vs 6.7% — all accurately reported, including the instability. Good work on the body text.

**Issue A. Headline claims the group difference the study failed to find** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Mothers who were maltreated as children feel like objects while breastfeeding — and it shows in the room"
- **Abstract says:** "evidence for the corresponding indirect association with observed maternal emotional availability differed across inferential methods… The omnibus distribution did not reach statistical significance (p = .244, Cramer's V = .29)"
- **Problem:** "And it shows in the room" asserts an observable maltreatment-linked difference in emotional availability — exactly the result that was non-significant and method-dependent. The self-objectification–EA association held; the maltreatment pathway to observed EA did not. The digest's own body and Caveats say so, so the headline contradicts them.
- **Suggested fix:** "Feeling like an object while breastfeeding: a pilot study links self-objectification to how mothers relate to their babies"

---

### Study 15: Self-harm in psychosis has different roots depending on whether the patient is in a forensic unit
**PMID:** 42711065 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

EU-VIORMED, five European countries, N = 392 aged 18–65 with SSD, LASSO logistic regression, lifetime DSH 45.9% forensic vs 39.5% non-forensic, forensic correlates (personality disorder β = 0.78, functional impairment), non-forensic correlates (interpersonal victimisation β = 0.85, personality disorder 0.71, male gender 0.69, substance use 0.37, PANSS items) — all accurate. Caveats correctly note that LASSO coefficients aren't effect sizes.

**Issue A. "Predicted" applied to a lifetime, cross-sectional outcome** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "in the non-forensic group, having been victimized by others predicted self-harm more strongly than any symptom of psychosis did"
- **Abstract says:** "Lifetime DSH was measured dichotomously… In non-forensic patients, interpersonal victimisation (β=0.85) was the strongest correlate"
- **Problem:** The comparison itself is right, but "predicted" implies temporal ordering that a lifetime dichotomous measure cannot supply — victimization and self-harm could have occurred in either order. The Caveats say correlates aren't causes; the pitch line reverts to predictive language.
- **Suggested fix:** "in the non-forensic group, a history of being victimized by others was more strongly associated with self-harm than any symptom of psychosis"

*Also note:* "Giovanni de Girolamo… who leads EU-VIORMED" is unverifiable from the abstract (he is senior author on this paper); confirm before pitching.

---

### Study 16: Racism and sexism push men and women toward addiction after trauma by opposite routes
**PMID:** 42708575 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 23 people of colour with co-occurring PTSD/SUD, qualitative interviews, the gendered accounts for women (sexism, sexual violence exposure, fear of being blamed or dismissed, substances to cope) and men (racism and exposure to gang/gun/interpersonal violence, "tough it out," criminalisation blocking help-seeking) all match. Caveats correctly limit the claim to hypothesis-generating testimony.

**Issue A. "Push" and "opposite routes" overstate a 23-person qualitative study** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Racism and sexism push men and women toward addiction after trauma by opposite routes"
- **Abstract says:** "racism and sexism influence the onset of men and women of color's PTSD/SUD in gendered ways… yet in distinctly gendered ways"
- **Problem:** "Push" reads as an established causal effect derived from participants' retrospective accounts, and "opposite routes" is stronger than "distinctly gendered" — the two pathways are different, not inverse. The authors' own language is already fairly strong, but the headline goes further on both counts.
- **Suggested fix:** "Racism and sexism shape the road into PTSD and addiction differently for men and women, survivors say"

---

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Many adults who score high on autism questionnaires… | ⚠️ Minor issues | Headline overweights childhood adversity; ACE did not distinguish groups |
| 2 | A genetic hunt for resilience finds a single variant… | ⚠️ Minor issues | P value shorthand wrong (3.08×10⁻⁸); NS fit 7 rests on fragile locus |
| 3 | People who struggle to name their feelings… | ⚠️ Minor issues | "And it isn't" asserts what authors say is undeterminable; 1-in-10 stat unsourced |
| 4 | Making patients relive their trauma works… | ❌ Significant issues | "Works" is an efficacy claim from a single-arm study; novelty label wrong; barrier claim unsupported |
| 5 | In Gaza, 94% of adults screen above… | ❌ Significant issues | "Most of the harm is structural" contradicts abstract's strongest predictor; headline generalizes sample; mediation range conflated |
| 6 | Recovery from disaster does not creep up… | ❌ Significant issues | Headline generalizes a pattern seen in ~6% of participants |
| 7 | Everyday racist stereotypes track how much physical pain… | ✅ Accurate | Numbers, framing and caveats all consistent with the abstract |
| 8 | Virtual reality role-play helps adults… | ❌ Significant issues | "Helps" causal from uncontrolled pilot; "first attempt" and "read faces" overstate |
| 9 | Shame, not guilt, is what cuts trauma survivors off… | ❌ Significant issues | Causal headline plus overgeneralized population; refugee framing unsupported |
| 10 | When a mother's trauma reaches her child… | ⚠️ Minor issues | "Travels through" is causal for a cross-sectional mediation |
| 11 | The trauma-exposed brain's sensory-to-thinking hierarchy… | ⚠️ Minor issues | Adult sample vs adolescent subgroup inconsistency; check full text before using the age angle |
| 12 | What actually protects child protection workers… | ⚠️ Minor issues | Turnover attributed to STS alone; abstract attributes it to both conditions |
| 13 | Teenagers who try suicide again are not flagged… | ⚠️ Minor issues | Pitch scene asserts risk forms "do not work"; authors conclude the opposite |
